html:
Tyrant of Athens, who seized power in 561 BCE, was twice driven out, and ruled securely from 546 BCE until his death in 527.

He first took power with a bodyguard granted after he showed wounds he claimed came from enemies. Once firmly in charge, he ruled mildly. He kept the laws of Solon in place, gave loans to small farmers and built up the city. Under him Athens gained:

  • new temples, including the start of the huge Temple of Olympian Zeus
  • a bigger Panathenaic festival and the City Dionysia, where tragedy was born
  • by later tradition, a written text of Homer's poems

His sons Hippias and Hipparchus took over. After Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus in 514, Hippias grew harsh and was expelled in 510. The reforms of Cleisthenes followed. Pisistratus' rule had made Athens more united and prosperous, preparing the ground for democracy.
sum: Tyrant of Athens, who seized power in 561 BCE, was twice driven out, and ruled securely from 546 BCE until his death in 527.
